name: Social democracy
summary: Social democracy is the family of socialist movements that pursue their aims by peaceful, parliamentary means within liberal democracy, split from communism over Bolshevik dictatorship, and came to seek a socially controlled, mixed market economy with a universal welfare state, strong unions and worker participation. Its own self-definition adds international solidarity, disarmament, development aid and equality between the sexes. The defining sources say little on most cultural, justice and constitutional questions.
scope: Family entry, answered only from sources that define the family as such: the Socialist International's Declaration of Principles (Stockholm 1989), the family's own international self-definition, which speaks of democratic socialism and names socialist, social democratic and labour parties as sharing its values; Michael Newman, Socialism: A Very Short Introduction (Oxford UP, 2005), the scholarly core (maintainer-supplied); and Kathleen Sears, Socialism 101 (Adams Media, 2019), a popular book used at medium confidence at most. Newman's Swedish case study, the SPD, Labour and other member parties' programmes and positions, expert surveys scoring parties, and Bernstein's own writings are not used, because members never answer for the family. Democratic socialism, Third Way, Nordic model and Eurocommunism have their own entries. Berman, Moschonas, Sassoon and Meyer were not available in full text and Britannica returned 403, so they are not cited. The Frankfurt Declaration (1951) could not be opened.

notes: Only a few dozen statements are settled by the defining sources: the Socialist International's Declaration covers democracy, economy, peace, development, gender and technology but is silent on healthcare, taxes, migration, religion-state questions and many others; Newman and Sears define the family mostly by its method (peaceful, constitutional) and its break with Bolshevism. Silence is null. Statements where the Declaration's general values (equal rights, freedom of belief) might bear on specific laws (apostasy, blasphemy, conversion) were left null.
